progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b06: barriers, inflammation, phagocytes and phagocytosis; dendritic cells carry pieces of a pathogen to a lymph node and show them to T cells; innate is fast and broad, adaptive is specific and takes days. From b01: bacteria are cells. From b03: bacteria grip host cells with surface threads (fimbriae); viruses use surface proteins to bind host cells. From Year 11: proteins have shapes that fit other molecules (enzyme and substrate); cells divide by mitosis into identical cells; DNA codes for proteins; the rough endoplasmic reticulum makes proteins for export. Not assumed: antigen, antibody structure, B cell receptors, clonal selection, clonal expansion, plasma cells, memory B cells, helper T cells (named only), the actions of antibodies.
progression.startsWith: Introduce antigens and matching receptors. The video opens: Your body can make antibodies that fit a bacterium it has never met before.
progression.stopsAfter: defining an antigen and explaining that receptors and antibodies bind one small part with a particular shape; describing the antibody (Y-shaped protein, two identical binding sites at the arm tips, a stem shared by many different antibodies) and that a B cell's receptors are antibodies held in its membrane; explaining that each B cell has one receptor shape and that billions of B cells with millions of shapes exist before infection because receptor genes are shuffled at random; explaining clonal selection (the antigen picks out the few B cells that already fit; usually a helper T cell's go-ahead is also needed); explaining clonal expansion and why a first response takes days; distinguishing plasma cells (release antibodies with the selected binding shape, which the blood carries to the infection) from memory B cells (stay for later); explaining how antibodies help without killing (block attachment and toxins, clump bacteria, coat them for phagocytes); explaining specific binding; interpreting a serum clumping experiment and evaluating a "design" claim.
progression.nextLesson: how T cells respond to infected cells (route entry bio-m7-b08).

teaching.task: Your body can make antibodies that fit a bacterium it has never met. How does it find the right B cells, and how do the antibodies they make target that bacterium?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why the body needn't design antibodies (the shapes already exist; hook, scene 5); why one cell has one shape and the body has millions (random gene shuffling during development; scene 5); why only some B cells respond (shape fit; scene 6); why a first response takes days (rare cells must multiply; scene 7 and attempt 2); why plasma cells make the right antibody (they release the selected receptor's shape; scenes 4 and 8); how binding helps without killing (block, clump, coat, linked back to b06's phagocytes; scene 9); what specific means (scene 10). Visible case: the same splinter bacterium from b06, and one B cell followed from the library to its clone. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scene 5 (row, shuffle diagram, field) and scene 9 (three panels) are the densest, so earlier parts dim at each cue.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Your body can make antibodies that fit a bacterium it has never met, and in 1957 Melbourne's Frank Macfarlane Burnet proposed that nothing is designed: the right cells already exist and the infection picks them out, so the question is how B cells find and target a pathogen. Following on from the dendritic cells of the last video, bacteria and their molecules reach a lymph node packed with lymphocytes, and this video follows the B cells. An antigen is a molecule the immune system can recognise, usually a protein or sugar chain on a pathogen's surface, and a receptor fits one small part of it. Each receptor is an antibody held in the membrane, a Y-shaped protein with a shared stem and two identical binding tips. Each B cell carries one receptor shape, made by random shuffling of receptor gene pieces in the bone marrow, so millions of shapes exist before any infection. Only the B cells that fit bind the antigen, usually with a helper T cell's go-ahead; that is selection, not instruction. The chosen cell divides over several days into a clone, which is why a first response takes days, and the clone becomes plasma cells that release antibodies and memory B cells that stay. Antibodies do not kill by themselves; they block attachment and toxins, link bacteria into clumps and coat them for phagocytes, and specific means each pathogen selects its own clones. The memory aid is clonal selection, the name is the process. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Your body can make antibodies that fit a bacterium it has never met before. So how does it design them in time? In 1957, the Melbourne scientist Frank Macfarlane Burnet proposed that it doesn't design anything. The right cells already exist before the infection, and the infection picks them out. That idea, clonal selection, explains how B cells target a pathogen.
teaching.understandingCheck: 13a explains a serum clumping result in two tubes (specific binding and antibody production, the route's stop). 13c evaluates the claim that B cells take a week because they must design an antibody (selection, rarity and expansion). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ3-01: "investigate and model the innate and adaptive immune systems in the human body (ACSBL119)". This video models the B cell (humoral) part of the adaptive system; b06 modelled the innate part, and b08 models the T cell part. Verb "investigate and model": the coded shape model of receptors and antigens (a deliberately simplified model, tagged as one) and the response strip are the model; attempt 1 investigates a serum experiment.

design.visualSystem: One lymph node board. Left two-thirds: painted cells (B cell, plasma cell, the bacterium, macrophage, T cell) with a coded shape model laid on them: each B cell's receptors are drawn as small coded Y shapes whose two tips carry one simple notch shape (triangle, round, square or wave), and the bacterium's antigens as small coded patches of matching shapes on its surface. A grey tag "model: receptors and antigens drawn far larger than real, shapes simplified" appears whenever the model is first used in a scene. Changes happen in place: the painted B cell crossfades to its aligned bare partner so coded receptors replace the painted ones exactly where they were (scene 5); the bare B cell crossfades to its aligned dividing partner before splitting (scene 7). Right third: b06's `ResponseStrip`, its first three rungs shrunk to grey thumbnails, the fourth rung ("days: adaptive", amber) expanded into five step chips filled as taught: "fit" (scene 6), "go-ahead" (scene 6), "clone" (scene 7), "plasma cells" (scene 8), "antibodies bind" (scene 9). No people, hands or faces: the body appears only as a lymph node, cells and molecules; the serum test in attempt 1 is a worded card with no tubes drawn. Coded elements are abstract only: the shape model, the response strip, a clone tree (branching lines with cell copies at the ends), a host cell membrane edge (as b03), a short day axis, arrows, chips and glosses. Scale: B cell about 8 µm, plasma cell about 12 to 15 µm, bacterium about 2 µm long, macrophage about 20 µm; the painted cells keep these proportions when shown together; antibodies (about 0.01 µm) are visible only as the enlarged coded model. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey labels; earlier chips dim to grey. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
